items.title: Small business survival rates are lower than commonly thought
items.claim: ONS UK Business Demography statistics consistently show what 5-year survival rate for new UK businesses?

options.text: Around 40% — roughly six in ten new UK businesses don't survive five years

items.reveal_title: Most new businesses don't make it
items.reveal:
ONS Business Demography data: of UK enterprises born in 2017, 39.6% survived to 2022. Year-1 survival is around 90%; the attrition is concentrated in years 2-5. SME failure causes (UK Federation of Small Businesses surveys) cluster around cash flow, late payment, and lack of management capacity.

Entrepreneurship narratives in business teaching focus on success stories. The base rate is more sobering and is one reason support programmes (start-up loans, mentoring) emphasise survival skills over growth.
items.why: Survivor bias in business case studies hides the failure rate. A textbook with only successful firms gives a misleading picture of what running a business actually involves.

items.title: First-mover advantage is more often a myth than a rule
items.claim: Gerard Tellis and Peter Golder studied first movers across 50 product categories. What did they find?

options.text: First movers won permanently in nearly all categories
About 47% of first movers failed and the average market share of survivors was around 10%; long-term winners were more often early followers than pioneers

items.reveal:
Tellis and Golder's 'Will and Vision' (2002) and earlier paper analysed product categories from photocopiers to disposable nappies. Pioneers identified: Chux nappies (replaced by Pampers); WordStar (overtaken by Word); Friendster and MySpace (overtaken by Facebook); AltaVista (overtaken by Google).

Later entrants benefit from market education done by pioneers, technology improvements, and clearer customer preferences. The 'first mover advantage' framing oversells a narrow set of cases (network-effect platforms) as if it were general.
items.why: Business teaching often treats first-mover advantage as a strategic prize. Empirical work suggests being the right mover at the right time is more important than being first.

items.title: Taylor's piece rate was an incentive, not a wage
items.claim: F.W. Taylor at Bethlehem Steel in the 1890s introduced piece-rate pay. What was the central design feature?

options.text: All workers received the same base pay regardless of output
Workers were paid per unit produced, with the 'scientific' target set so only those following Taylor's prescribed method could earn the bonus
Piece rates were determined by union negotiation

items.reveal_title: Pay per piece, conditional on method
items.reveal:
Taylor's pig-iron handling experiments at Bethlehem Steel (1898-99) raised loading from 12.5 to 47 tons per worker per day. Workers earning the bonus received about 60% more pay; the firm got 280% more output per worker.

Unions opposed Taylorism fiercely — 1911 US Congressional hearings investigated 'speed-up' abuses. Modern piece rates persist in garment factories, gig economy (Uber surge pricing as a variant) and sales commissions.
items.why: Piece rates align effort with output but can erode quality, safety and worker autonomy. The same design principle reappears in 'pay for performance' compensation a century later.
